tales-of-the-jazz-age: F. Scott Fitzgerald's 1922 collection captures the glitter and ache of his generation. The Curious Case of Benjamin Button, The Diamond as Big as the Ritz, and other stories mix fantasy, satire, and heartbreak. These are the tales that made Fitzgerald the voice of the Jazz Age — brilliant, restless, and already tinged with loss.
grace-harlowe-s-second-year-at-overton-c: Josephine Chase follows Grace Harlowe through her sophomore year at Overton College — new friendships, college pranks, and the small tests of character that shape young women. The Grace Harlowe books were beloved by generations of schoolgirls. Wholesome, spirited college life as readers once dreamed it.
the-little-savage: Captain Marryat's adventure maroons a boy on a desert island, where he grows up wild — a savage by circumstance, not nature. His rescue and return to civilization test what upbringing really means. Exciting and thought-provoking, from the master of the sea story.
the-children-s-pilgrimage: L. T. Meade — the beloved author of countless girls' books — tells of children on a pilgrimage of the heart, learning faith and courage along the way. Her stories guided generations of young readers. Tender, moral, and written with real understanding of children.
english-men-of-letters-coleridge: H. D. Traill profiles Samuel Taylor Coleridge — poet of the Ancient Mariner, philosopher, and opium-haunted genius — for the English Men of Letters series. Sympathetic and acute, the study captures both the glory and the tragedy. A fine short biography of a complex great man.
birds-in-town-village: W. H. Hudson finds birds in town and village — the swifts, sparrows, and nightingales of English streets and lanes. His loving observations make familiar birds wonderful. A gentle classic of bird lore. Even London sparrows become marvelous under his patient eye.
a-crystal-age: W. H. Hudson's strange and lovely utopia pictures a far future of pastoral peace — no money, no strife, only gentle folk living close to nature. His dream of simplicity rebukes our hurried modern world. A beautiful, haunting vision from the author of Green Mansions.
the-awkward-age: Henry James' Awkward Age studies Nanda Brookenham, a clever girl coming of age among worldly elders in London society. His intricate, glittering dialogue reveals a whole social world. James at his most brilliantly analytical — demanding, dazzling fiction. Vanderbank, Mr. Longdon, and the Brookethams circle her with civilized danger.
